main was RED. `unit-swarm-call-fixture.test.ts`'s pin asserts the exact set of value
exports from both strategy modules, and SealSideDoor's publication-seal work landed
four more — PUBLICATION_SURFACES, PUBLISHING_CARRIES, admitsPublication,
carrySuppression. Neither side is wrong: the pin is doing what it was built to do,
which is notice that the module's surface changed.

The four are LISTED rather than excluded by a filter. The pin exists to go red when a
preset-to-config table, a validity predicate, a verifier-kind registry or a call parser
lands, and the seal exports are none of those — so naming them keeps the pin sensitive
to what it is actually for, while loosening it to "starts with SWARM_ or is one of these
two" would have made it blind to exactly what it watches. Widening a check to make it

why: the orchestrator and a subagent both credited: "Main's three decisions, plus AxisErgonomics' final numbers"
message:
docs(exploration): bind judgeSamples to the judge branch, name the wire form, and
rename the one value measurement found unusable

Main's three decisions, plus AxisErgonomics' final numbers. Both of his first two were
already implemented when the message arrived; his DECISION 2 wording is more precise
than mine and is taken over it.

DECISION 1 — judgeSamples moves onto the judge-scored branch of a discriminated
`score`. The table declaring it `—` for all five presets could not be constructed for
ANY row while the field was required (TS2741, compiler-proven by FixtureZero) — so the
table that is normatively resolve(preset) -> SwarmConfig was unexpressible as the type
it resolves to. Of the three ways out only tagging makes the invalid state
unrepresentable: optional reintroduces a gate firing on an absent input, and inheriting
3 ships four of five presets below the bar with no record of whether 3 was chosen or
inherited. Same move as Measurement having no fault member and as subordinates/depth.ts
making a child's depth unstateable — the number a config would have to lie about is one
it never supplies. It also dissolves the fourth instalment of the caps-versus-axes
finding rather than paying it: bind the parameter to the value that uses it and there is
no separate field left to be inexpressible.

Applied exhaustively per section 6.1, with its one honest exception stated: carry's
admission thresholds are tagged too, while pruneThreshold/minVisitsForPrune span the
REGION of tree selectors rather than one value, so they cannot be tagged and their
applicability must be CHECKED rather than assumed — supplying them under
archive/pareto/none is a refusal, because a parameter accepted and ignored is a lie
about what the run did.

DECISION 2 — the canonical digest form is the WIRE form, computed after normalisation,
once, because it is the only form both caller and registry provably see. For `spec` the
wire form and the received bytes coincide, which is what makes it safe: spec is opaque
to the objective's naming convention (the convention governs the fields this spec
declares, not the interior of a payload whose schema the registered kind owns) AND the
harness must not transform it. With no transform there are not two sides for two honest
implementations to disagree about. stableStringify fixes key ORDER and says nothing
about key SPELLING, which is why this needed saying.

DECISION 3 — section 6.5 was prescribing a NO-OP and now names the binding cap.
JudgeCeiling measured actual judge calls on shipped defaults: requested 3/4/20 all
realise 3 on a code branch, because the ceiling is min(judgeSamples,
maxEvalLLMCalls - 1) — one of the four calls buys the generated check suite. So "raise
judgeSamples", which this paragraph used to advise, does nothing. The sharpest fact is
that the default request already sits FLUSH against the ceiling, so the first step a
caller takes toward a better ensemble is the step that silently does nothing — and
against 28.5-versus-30.0 a reader following the old advice could not get above the knee
by doing what it said. Reaching 20 needs maxEvalLLMCalls >= 21, measured at 4.2x every
search and still under the $10 gate, so nothing refuses it; it just costs 4.2x quietly.
The ceiling table is cited from docs/MCTS.md rather than restated so the two cannot
drift. Whether a default moves is a spend decision and not this spec's to make.

THE ONE RENAME MEASUREMENT ARGUES FOR: decorrelate:'fresh' -> 'blind'. 0/6 on a reverse
probe, read as RECENCY by both vendors shown the bare name, and 4 of its 10 in-context
uses described the `angles` mechanism instead with the gloss in front of the model —
three instruments, six families. `angles` STAYS despite scoring 2/6 bare, because it was
correct in all 29 in-context uses, and `carry` stays for the same reason at 23/24: a
name is only read beside the question it answers, so a bare-probe failure is a
documentation constraint and not a rename.

And a disclosure gap I never closed, measured at 18%: models correctly identify
unit:'trajectory' for an agent-search task, the design says that combination is BLOCKED,
and nothing on the surface said so. A caller who composes the blocked shape CORRECTLY
and is told nothing has been failed by the surface rather than the axes. Now a call-time
refusal with one imperative. Named as a class, because it has appeared three times: the
seal covered one table while five channels published past it, the guard covered names
while inline source walked through, and a blocked composition lived in a design note
instead of on the surface. In every case the property was real and the caller could not
see it.

Study figures re-cited to the final run throughout: 280 configure calls, seven model
families, 245 answered, refusals 24/24.

why: a 135-character subject wrapped across two physical lines, plus two credited subagents
message:
docs(exploration): one digest rule instead of two that rhyme, and the guard that
cannot fire on the channel carrying model-written code

Main's two corrections to FixtureZero's findings, plus a live bug I reproduced.

G6 — CLOSING THE CLOSURE ARM AND LEAVING `kind` UNDIGESTED JUST MOVES THE HOLE BEHIND
A PICKLIST. The closure arm died because Function.prototype.toString() returns a body
and not its captured environment: the digest could not see what the name resolved to.
argumentDigest({kind, spec}) has the identical defect one level up — two runs sharing
a kind, with the registry re-pointed between them, digest identically and are not
comparable. Stating those as two clauses that happen to agree would have left the
second open, so section 5.1 now states one rule: an identity that NAMES an
implementation must digest WHAT THE NAME RESOLVES TO, or it is not an identity. A name
is a claim the caller can get wrong; a name whose referent can change is a claim the
SYSTEM can get wrong, which is worse because nobody typed it. verifierDigest therefore
covers kind, spec, and a digest of the registry entry kind resolves to. The test that
it is one rule and not two: it is the VerifierSpec argument with "registry entry"
substituted for "closure".

G7 — SECURITY-ADJACENT, NOT A DOCUMENTATION NIT, AND IT IS THE SEAL'S SIDE DOOR ONE
SECTION OVER. Section 4.4 stated a property over records-store writes while
experience_library published past it; section 3.4 states a guard over NAMES while
inline SOURCE walks through. Same shape: the property is stated over one channel and
the dangerous channel is not among the ones it quantifies over — which is why the seal
needed an enumeration and why this needs a per-kind declaration. And there is no
approval gate named for verifier-supplied source though this repo has one for shell,
so executable text crosses a model-facing boundary into exec with a guard that provably
cannot fire on it. The finding is not that the guard is weak but that the one channel
it cannot protect is the one carrying code a model wrote.

G3/G13 — REPRODUCED RATHER THAN ACCEPTED, AND IT IS A MONEY BUG.
parseAgentsToolInput({action:'fork', task:'x', budgetUsd:5, wallClockMs:1000}) returns
{action:'fork', task:'x'}: both caps gone. A model asks for a $5 ceiling and gets no
ceiling, silently, today. That is section 2.1's failure on the one surface where
silence costs money, and it is the same defect shape as the rest — an unknown key is
DROPPED where it should be REFUSED. A dropped cap is not a default cap, it is an
unmetered run, which is absent-is-not-zero applied to spend instead of to a column. So
the parser MUST refuse an unrecognised key with bad_input naming the key and the
spelling it expected, and the spec says why that is a precondition rather than a
hardening: every guarantee here is stated over what the caller ASKED FOR.

It also settles objective's wire spelling, which the composition made urgent. The
types are camelCase because that is correct TypeScript; the tool surface is snake_case,
so objective's wire form is snake_case and the mapping is contract rather than
implementation detail. An objective that were the one camelCase island in a snake_case
action would make camelCase-for-snake_case the EXPECTED model error rather than an
exotic one.

G9 was already closed in the previous commit — the preset tuple table is normatively
resolve(preset) -> SwarmConfig rather than an illustration of one.

why: a prefix outside the vocabulary ("lean"), an 81-character subject, and "this session"
message:
lean(gate): check the citation direction nobody checked, and fix three stale ones

`check-traceability.mjs` proved Lean -> TypeScript: every claimed theorem is
declared, every `tsRef` resolves to a real line. Nothing proved TypeScript ->
Lean. So `mcts/engine.ts:11` reading "Formal spec: MCTS/StorageIsolation.lean -
init_isolated, transition_preserves_isolation" was unchecked prose - delete the
theorem and the header still claims it - and PR-MCTS-003's own `tsRefs` point at
three other files entirely. A citation with no checker is a comment that reads
like a guarantee, which is the defect class this session has been about.

IT WAS NOT HYPOTHETICAL. On introduction the gate found three stale citations
that every existing gate had passed:

- `mcts/schemas.ts:6` and `types/mcts.ts:7` both cited
  `MCTS/Backpropagation.lean:initial_valid`. The Float-to-scaled-integer rewrite
  renamed that theorem to `initial_in_range`; `docs/MCTS.md:336` already tracks
  the new name, so the two source headers were the only stale copies.
- `unit-consolidation.test.ts:3` cited `CraftStore.lean - all_below_gives_empty,
  consolidation_requires_nonempty_guard`. Neither name has ever existed in any
  module, and `CraftStore.lean` holds only `consolidate_keeps_above` and
  `search_length_bound`. The theorems that actually cover what that suite tests
  live in `Evolution/FullCraftLifecycle.lean`, which is what the file it tests
  (`craft/consolidation.ts:5`) already cites. Corrected to match.

WHY A SEPARATE PROGRAM RATHER THAN MORE OF `check-traceability.mjs`. The check
needs the corpus from `sources.ts`, the repository's single enumeration, and the
declarations from the Lean scanner that `.mjs` already owns. It cannot have both
in one file: the anti-slop `RAW_NODE_MODULE` boundary is measured over the
plugin's own entrypoints via `import-extension.gate.test.ts`, and widening it for
a Lean gate would be exactly the "a gate measured one set and governed another"
defect `sources.ts` documents. So the declarations cross as a subprocess's stdout
under a new `--list-declarations` mode. One scanner, two consumers, no second
spelling of either the file enumeration or the Lean parser.

Three failure directions, each proven red->green by hand before wiring: a cited
theorem that no module declares, a cited theorem declared in a DIFFERENT module
from the one named, and a cited module that does not exist. Resolution accepts
the three path spellings already in the tree plus bare basenames, because
`docs/MCTS.md` and the exploration spec cite `StorageIsolation.lean` unprefixed;
an ambiguous basename fails rather than guessing. A cited name must be
snake_case, which is load-bearing rather than cosmetic - the colon form runs into
prose, so `runtime.ts:1056`'s "StorageIsolation.lean: branch storage disjoint"
would otherwise report `branch` as a missing theorem - and `CITATION_OPAQUE`
ratchets the one resulting blind spot so a new underscore-free theorem fails the
gate naming itself instead of quietly joining it.

Wired into `verify-lean.sh`, so it runs in both Lean workflows and in the
required deploy gate. 39 module and 21 theorem citations governed across 1365
files.

docs(exploration): close four gaps found by measurement, not by review

AxisErgonomics ran 160 configure calls over four vendors against the rendered
surface. Three of its findings are spec defects I would not have found by
reading, and the fourth is the owner's floor-continuation question answered.

`advance:'pareto'` had nowhere to put its objectives. `objective` was singular,
so a front was unreachable from the surface while the coverage matrix claimed
GEPA was expressible — and asked for a frontier over six eval metrics a model
said so outright: "the six specific eval metrics are not provided; the search
would need a way to compute each metric for a candidate". One `verify` string
cannot carry six. So `Objective` gains `VectorObjective`, `advance:'pareto'`
requires it with two or more components, and a scalar plus pareto is refused
because a front over one dimension is an argmax. Two independent routes reached
this field: the design doc had already noted AlphaEvolve is FunSearch with an
evaluator returning a score DICT, and this is that dict.

That defect also exposed a hole in the coverage obligation itself, so it gains a
sixth property: every fixture entry must be REACHABLE FROM `SwarmInput`. Pareto
satisfied all five existing properties while no caller could express it.
Expressible-in-the-fixture and expressible-by-a-caller are different claims and
only the second is worth anything.

The static refusal on a missing verifier catches almost nothing, and the receipt
is unambiguous. Given "optimise our onboarding copy so more people finish
signup", where no number is reachable from inside a run, gemini-3-flash answered
`verify:'python3 scripts/simulate_conversion.py --copy-file candidate_copy.txt'`
for a script that does not exist. A rule that fires on a MISSING field cannot
fire when the caller fabricates one to satisfy it. The call-time check is now
documented as ADVISORY and the `unavailable` fault at the baseline measurement as
THE guard. The residual is stated rather than implied: the fault catches a
fabricated instrument, never a fabricated objective, and both vendors produced a
fabricated objective for Collatz — one measuring the final value of the sequence,
one maximising steps-before-reaching-1, which is a real surrogate that still does
not test the conjecture. Section 2.4(c) predicted exactly that and no mechanical
check here detects it.

Width had nowhere to go, which was a hole my own preset decision created. With
`branches` inside `config`, a named preset — which takes no `config` — could not
say "eight candidates", and models reported the absence unprompted across
vendors. `branches` and `depth` are resource caps, not axes: ToT at branches=3
and ToT at branches=8 are the same technique, whereas uct versus beam is not. So
they move to `SwarmInput` where every preset takes them, which follows the line
section 6.4 already drew rather than bending it.

And the floor-breach hole is closed: the run CONTINUES, publication HALTS. The
two hypotheses a breach admits demand opposite responses — re-derive the bound,
or close a gap in the measured channel — and a breach cannot tell them apart, so
halting would discard sound work over a bound that is itself under suspicion
while publishing would launder a number someone will quote. The floor is
suspended for the rest of the run and recorded as suspended; publication is
sealed for that objective until a human re-derives it; nothing else clears the
seal, because neither a retry nor a later in-bound measurement is evidence about
which hypothesis was true. Stated as reachability rather than as a guard — a
records-store write requires `PublicationState` open — so S7 strengthens from
"writes nothing" to "publication is unreachable".

Also measured, and the cleanest vindication in the set: across 200 calls no model
invented a `subject`-shaped field. Models complained loudly about the two
absences that became changes above; the silence on `subject` is the useful kind.
Section 11 gains three gaps that are now known rather than suspected.

why: CONTROL, must pass: legal prefix, 72-character subject, and the legitimate product possessive "Nimbus's own npm"
message:
feat(workspace): install bash and python into the workspace on first use

The agent's own workspace answered 127 to `python3`, `pip`, `bash`, `npm` and
`npx`. Not disabled — ABSENT: a bare `NimbusWorkspace` is the JavaScript half of
Nimbus, and nothing had been handed to it that could run a wasm module or reach
a package registry.

Both halves are the substrate's own. `seedRuntimePackage` writes a runtime
package into the filesystem at the same path `nimbus install` writes on
Cloudflare, from the same manifest, digest-verified — the core calls it "the
second publisher, not the second package manager", and which one ran is not
observable afterwards. `createNpmCommand`/`createNpxCommand` are Nimbus's own npm
client. The bytes are two npm packages, so `@proteus/core` never imports them:
the host that has a filesystem supplies them, which keeps 40 MB of wasm and a
`node:fs` read out of the Worker.

Provisioned on FIRST USE of the command, never at open. Measured by
scripts/nimbus-runtime-probe.ts: open is 19ms with nothing supplied and 28ms
with both, the first `python3` costs 113ms because it IS the install, and every
one after it costs 0ms. Re-seeding an installed runtime is 0.2ms, so the expense
was never the check — it is the 35.7 MB of durable rows CPython writes, which a
workspace that never runs Python must not carry.

Verbatim, same probe, same workspace, through `createWorkspace` as
`createCLIRuntime` opens it:

  before  exit 127  python3 --version   python3: command not found
  after   exit   0  python3 --version   Python 3.13.14 (CPython, wasm32-wasi, Nimbus runtime)
  before  exit 127  pip --version       pip: command not found
  after   exit   0  pip --version       pip 24.3.1 (Nimbus package bridge for CPython 3.13, wasm32-wasi)
  before  exit 127  bash --version      bash: command not found
  after   exit   0  bash --version      GNU bash, version 5.2.37(1)-release (wasm32-unknown-wasi)
  before  exit 127  npm --version       npm: command not found
  after   exit   0  npm --version       10.0.0

The capability the executor declares is derived from the same list that decides
which commands get registered, so the declaration cannot drift from the registry:
a host that supplies nothing declares nothing extra.

Still 127, and named rather than papered over: `git` (@nimbus-sh/core ships none
at all — it lives in @nimbus-sh/worker, which needs a Durable Object and is not
a core dependency), `bun` (no runtime package exists; the hosted session's own
runner serves it), and `sh`/`make`/`tsc`/`jq`, which exist on neither path.

why: CONTROL, must pass: legal prefix and "Cloudflare's @cloudflare/sandbox SDK"
message:
fix(sandbox): retry transient errors + broadcast failures + image bump

Phase 1 sandbox resilience — closes STABILITY-AUDIT §B2, §B3, §B4, §B5.

B2/B3 — retry wrapper for transient SDK + DO-RPC errors
  Added withRetry() helper around every handle.* call (exec, readFile,
  writeFile, listFiles, deleteFile, exists, exposePort, unexposePort,
  getExposedPorts) in packages/core/src/execution/sandbox.ts. Retries
  twice (3 attempts total) on lower-cased error messages containing:
    - 'network connection lost'    (DO-to-DO RPC drop, not retried by SDK)
    - 'container suddenly disconnected'  (mid-request 500, not retried)
    - 'container is starting'      (cold-start 503-mapped — defense in depth)
    - 'no container instance'      (provisioning)
    - 'http error! status: 500'    (catches the SDK's wrapped 500 form)
  Backoff: 500ms × 2^attempt (so 0ms, 500ms, 1000ms). Non-transient
  errors throw immediately so genuine bugs aren't masked.

  Why this matters: Cloudflare's @cloudflare/sandbox SDK only auto-retries
  HTTP 503 responses. A mid-request container migration surfaces as a
  500 with body 'Container suddenly disconnected, try again' which the
  SDK does NOT retry — so 'Network connection lost' bubbled all the way
  to the agent's tool result string. The withRetry wrapper closes that
  gap by treating the documented transient markers as auto-retryable.

B4 — broadcast on error path
  orchestrator.ts:executeInExecutor catch block now emits the same
  'executor-output' broadcast as the success branch, with stderr=errMsg
  and exitCode=1. Without this, a user typing a command that hit a
  transient error saw a blank prompt because the xterm terminal renders
  only from broadcasts; the RPC return value is discarded.

B5 — container image SDK skew
  wrangler.jsonc: cloudflare/sandbox 0.8.10 → 0.8.11 to match the JS
  SDK version installed in node_modules. 0.8.11 ships transient-error
  detection improvements that work in tandem with the retry wrapper.

Tests: 102 pass / 3 skip / 0 fail.

why: CONTROL, must pass: "Vite's `?raw` text import", and a subject that IS a binary contrast — a shape this gate deliberately does not judge
message:
chore(modules): an import specifier names a module, not a build output

Nothing here emits. Every project sets `noEmit`, no `outDir` exists in the
tree, and all three runtimes read the TypeScript directly: Vite and wrangler
bundle the Worker from source, Bun runs the CLI and every suite from source,
and the deploy publishes a CLI source archive with a checksum rather than a
build. AGENTS.md nonetheless mandated ".js extension (ESM convention, even for
.ts source files)", and that produced 3,325 specifiers naming files that have
never existed. They resolved only because a bundler was willing to guess, and
`scripts/` had already drifted to 82 `.ts` against 94 `.js` with nothing to
stop it — which is what a convention with no enforcement looks like.

TWO REGIMES, BECAUSE THERE ARE GENUINELY TWO RESOLVERS. Bundled-or-Bun code
takes no extension: both resolvers find `./x` for `./x.ts` and the extension
carries no information. `tools/oxlint/anti-slop/**` plus `scripts/sources.ts`
keep explicit `.ts`, because oxlint's RuleTester needs Node's raw transfer and
throws under Bun — measured, not assumed — and Node's ESM resolver takes a
complete path, resolving neither a missing extension nor a directory index.
That closure is 62 files at this commit and it is measured, not listed:
`import-extension.gate.test.ts` recomputes it from the `node` entrypoints in
`package.json` and fails naming any file that enters or leaves it.

`.js` is gone. The twelve that remain name files that are really on disk —
`packages/pc-agent/src/index.js` is a genuinely CommonJS package, and seven
point into a dependency's own `dist/`.

tsconfig, each setting defended by what breaks without it:
  - `allowImportingTsExtensions` removed from eight projects and deliberately
    NOT hoisted to the base. Measured: removing it costs zero errors outside
    the two projects holding closure files, and exactly one (TS5097,
    sources.ts:45) inside them. Its absence is what makes a stray `.ts`
    specifier a type error and not merely a lint error.
  - `verbatimModuleSyntax` added to the base. cf-backend already ran with it
    via `agents/tsconfig`; moving that package onto our base without it would
    have silently downgraded the one package Vite actually bundles. Zero
    errors across all twelve projects.
  - `module` stays `ESNext`. `Preserve` was measured and changes nothing here
    (0 errors either way); its distinguishing behaviours — `require()` in ESM,
    decoupling `allowImportingTsExtensions` from `noEmit` — are unused. Adding
    it would be cargo-cult.
  - cf-backend now extends `tsconfig.base.json` instead of `agents/tsconfig`.
    Inheriting out of node_modules meant our own base did not govern the
    Worker: it ran at ES2021 without `resolveJsonModule`, and a dependency
    bump could have moved its module settings.

Four resolvers in the tree assumed the old spelling and are fixed, not
worked around: `gate-set-equality.localImports` and `unit-layergate`'s
`resolveImport` both rewrote a trailing `.js` and returned nothing for an
extensionless specifier, which walks no edges and silently shrinks the set
the gate exists to compare; `capability-parity` carried a now-dead `.jsx?`
strip; `layergate --lock` GENERATED `from './gate.js'` into a real file.
Four source-text assertions naming the old spelling are updated.

The rule is `anti-slop/require-runtime-import-extension`, registered the way
the others are and proven red in both directions through the real binary. It
checks the filesystem rather than guessing, so a `.mjs` fixture, a `.json`
import and Vite's `?raw` text import of the CommonJS daemon all stay legal —
the defect is a specifier naming a file that is not there, which is exactly
what it reports. `scripts/sources.ts` exposes the boundary as
`isRawNodeModule`, the same direction `TEST_FILE` already travels, so a gate
asks the ONE enumeration instead of writing a path pattern of its own.

Verified: `bun run check` exit 0; core 3414/3 skip, cf-backend 1176,
cli-backend 299, cli 607, test-utils 153, compaction 95, agent-utils 15,
scripts 354, workerd 7/7 — the three residual failures are byte-identical on
c3a8e220 and predate this branch; `test:anti-slop` green under raw Node; all
twelve gate programs, layergate and tracing-gate exit 0; the CLI starts and
lists six real workspaces; `vite build` in cf-backend completes.
